title: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

blocks.text: For awaitable I/O, use async def and await. For a blocking I/O library, use a normal def handler; FastAPI runs that path operation in an external thread pool.
An async def path operation runs asynchronously. An ordinary helper called directly from it is not automatically moved to the thread pool. A blocking call there can block the event loop.

nodes.label: def path operation — external thread pool
Direct ordinary helper call inside async def
Blocking call remains on event loop; can block it

blocks.alt_text: Three execution paths distinguish awaitable I/O, thread-pool-backed normal def handlers, and blocking utilities called directly inside async handlers.

steps.title: Follow the call into the helper

blocks.text: The registered shipping client performs blocking I/O. A normal def path operation places that work in FastAPI’s external thread pool. An awaitable library would instead suit async def with awaited operations.

Moving blocking I/O into an ordinary utility does not change its execution boundary. Called directly from async def, that utility is not automatically offloaded and can block the event loop. Trace the call, not just the handler’s spelling.

segments.label: How FastAPI executes def and async def handlers
segments.summary: FastAPI automatically runs a normal def path operation in a separate thread pool, allowing the main event loop to continue processing other requests. An async def path operation runs on the event loop itself, where blocking I/O can stop other work from progressing. A normal def handler is therefore a valid execution choice, not inherently a wrong or slow one.

blocks.group_title: Handler execution and the event-loop boundary

bridge.before: Watch for the execution boundary of each handler. Interpret the clip’s instruction to await I/O as applying to awaitable operations; adding await does not make a blocking library asynchronous.
bridge.after: The clip distinguishes handler execution modes but does not teach library-based selection or ordinary-helper dispatch. The text covers both: choose by I/O behavior, and trace directly called helpers within the handler’s execution boundary.

public.prompt: An async def handler directly calls a normal utility that performs blocking I/O. What does FastAPI do with this direct utility call?

options.text: It is not automatically offloaded; the blocking call can block the event loop.
The utility becomes awaitable solely because its caller is async def.
It automatically offloads every normal utility called by async def.

o1.message: FastAPI runs a normal def path operation in an external thread pool, whereas an async def path operation runs as asynchronous execution. FastAPI does not automatically move ordinary utility functions called directly by a handler to a thread pool; a blocking call inside async def can block the event loop.

o2.message: A normal utility is not made awaitable by an async caller; its blocking I/O remains blocking.

o3.message: Automatic thread-pool execution for normal path operations does not apply to arbitrary direct utility calls.

steps.title: Practice: Choosing def versus async def from I/O behavior without blocking the event loop

public.prompt: Choose normal def for the supplied blocking operation, without awaiting it. Preserve the direct shipping_utility() call and return the supplied shipping result. Fill execution_trace with the FastAPI execution location for both the handler and its directly called ordinary utility (use "external thread pool" or "event loop"). Request GET /verify-shipping to check the declaration, logical execution trace, and result. Keep the supplied verification harness unchanged: this threadless sandbox checks the trace by inspection and calls the handler directly; it does not measure worker-thread execution.

files.content:
from fastapi import FastAPI
import time

class BlockingShippingClient:
    """Synthetic blocking I/O stand-in; no network access."""
    def lookup(self):
        time.sleep(0.01)
        return {"status": shipping_status}

shipping_status = 'synthetic-shipping-result'
shipping_client = BlockingShippingClient()

app = FastAPI()

def shipping_utility():
    return shipping_client.lookup()

@app.get("/shipping")
async def shipping():  # TODO: choose execution mode for blocking I/O.
    return shipping_utility()

execution_trace = {"handler": None, "utility": None}  # TODO: fill both execution locations.

# Supplied declaration/trace verification harness: leave unchanged.
# The sandbox has no worker threads: check the declaration and a logical trace,
# then call the handler directly to check result preservation. This is not a
# measurement of actual worker-thread execution.
import inspect

async def verify_shipping():
    assert not inspect.iscoroutinefunction(shipping), "Use a normal def for blocking I/O"
    assert not inspect.iscoroutinefunction(shipping_utility), "Preserve the ordinary utility"
    assert execution_trace["handler"] == 'external thread pool', "Trace the handler's FastAPI execution boundary"
    assert execution_trace["utility"] == execution_trace["handler"], "A direct utility call shares the handler boundary"
    return shipping()

app.add_api_route("/verify-shipping", verify_shipping, methods=["GET"])
